title: Module 2: Divide and Conquer, Merge Sort, and Recursion Trees

questions.q: What are the three steps of a Divide and Conquer algorithm, in order?
questions.explain: Divide the problem into smaller subproblems, Conquer them (usually recursively), then Combine their solutions into a solution to the original problem.

questions.q: Which Divide and Conquer step usually solves the smaller subproblems recursively? (one word)
questions.explain: Conquer: solve the smaller problems, usually by solving them recursively.

questions.q: In Merge Sort, what happens during the Combine step?
choices: The two sorted halves are merged into one sorted array
The array is split into a first half and a second half
Each subarray is checked to see whether it has one element
questions.explain: Divide = split into halves, Conquer = recursively sort each half, Combine = MERGE the two sorted halves.

questions.q: What is Merge Sort's base case, and why does it need no work?
choices: A subarray with one element, because a single element is already sorted
A subarray with two elements, because one comparison sorts it
An empty array, because MERGE skips it
A subarray of size log₂ n, because that is the height of the tree
questions.explain: Merge Sort keeps dividing until every subproblem has one element. A single element is already sorted.

questions.q: In Divide and Conquer, the subproblems are smaller instances of the same problem as the original.
questions.explain: The key feature is recursion: the algorithm solves smaller instances of the same problem until an instance is small enough to solve directly.

questions.q: Merge Sort is dividing 8 3 5 4 7 6 1 2. Which line shows the pieces after the second round of division?
questions.explain: Round 1 gives 8 3 5 4 | 7 6 1 2. Round 2 halves each piece: 8 3 | 5 4 | 7 6 | 1 2. Nothing is sorted yet; sorting happens only during merging.

questions.q: Merge Sort runs on 5 4 1 8 7 2 6 3. Which two sorted arrays go into the final merge?
questions.explain: The first half 5 4 1 8 becomes [4 5] and [1 8], then [1 4 5 8]. The second half 7 2 6 3 becomes [2 7] and [3 6], then [2 3 6 7].

questions.q: Merge Sort runs on 8 3 5 4 7 6 1 2. After the single elements are merged into pairs, which four sorted pairs exist?
questions.explain: Each pair comes from merging two neighboring single elements: 8,3 -> 3 8; 5,4 -> 4 5; 7,6 -> 6 7; 1,2 -> 1 2.

questions.q: Merge Sort runs on 8 3 5 4 7 6 1 2. Which two sorted arrays go into the final merge?
questions.explain: [3 8] and [4 5] merge to [3 4 5 8]. [6 7] and [1 2] merge to [1 2 6 7]. The final merge gives 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8.

questions.q: In MERGESORT, the two recursive calls do the comparing and placing of elements, and MERGE only joins the two halves end to end.
questions.explain: The recursive calls only split the array and recurse. All of the comparisons and placements happen inside MERGE.

questions.q: Merge the sorted arrays A = [1, 4, 7, 9] and B = [2, 3, 5, 8]. What is the result?
questions.explain: Compare the front elements each time: 1v2->1, 4v2->2, 4v3->3, 4v5->4, 7v5->5, 7v8->7, 9v8->8. B is now used up, so copy the 9.

questions.q: MERGE runs on C = [4, 5] and D = [1, 8]. What value is written to B[2]?
questions.explain: k=1: 4 vs 1, so B[1]=1 (from D). k=2: 4 vs 8, so B[2]=4 (from C).

questions.q: In MERGE, the else branch (taken when D[j] is the smaller front element) contains the line B[k] = ___ followed by j++. What fills the blank?
questions.explain: The else branch copies the smaller element from D, which is D[j]. That is why it then increments j. Writing C[j] is a common transcription error.

questions.q: In MERGE, what does the loop variable k index?
choices: The next position to fill in the output array B
The smallest unused element of C
The smallest unused element of D
The current level of the recursion tree
questions.explain: i points into C, j points into D, and k is the next output position in B.

questions.q: During a merge, array C runs out of elements while D still has some left. What should happen?
choices: Copy the rest of D into B in order
Stop, because B is already complete
Sort the rest of D again before copying it
Compare D's remaining elements against C's last element
questions.explain: D is already sorted, and everything left in it is at least as large as everything already placed. So the rest of D is copied into B in order.

questions.q: MERGE combines two sorted arrays whose combined length is n = 10. How many times does its for loop run?
questions.explain: The loop runs for k = 1 to n and fills one output position per iteration, so it runs n = 10 times.

questions.q: MERGE runs on C = [1, 4, 7, 9] and D = [2, 3, 5, 8]. Which element is placed without any comparison because the other array is already used up?
questions.explain: After 8 is placed, D is used up. The remaining 9 from C is copied directly.

questions.q: Count MERGE's operations as 2 setup operations plus 4 per loop iteration (4n + 2 in total). How many operations does it do for a combined length of n = 10?
Which fact justifies the inequality 4l + 2 ≤ 6l for every integer l ≥ 1?
questions.explain: Since l ≥ 1, 2 ≤ 2l. Add 4l to both sides: 4l + 2 ≤ 4l + 2l = 6l.

questions.q: Why replace the exact count 4l + 2 with the looser bound 6l?
choices: 6l is still a valid upper bound, and a single term is much easier to multiply and add across the recursion tree
6l is the exact count once the base case is included
6l is a lower bound, and a lower bound is what the running-time proof needs
questions.explain: The bound is slightly looser but much easier to work with. It is a deliberate trade of a little accuracy for tractability.

questions.q: Lemma 1 says that for two sorted arrays C and D of length l/2 each, MERGE performs at least 6l operations.
questions.explain: Lemma 1 is an upper bound: MERGE performs at most 6l operations.

questions.q: Which of these are counted as operations in each iteration of MERGE's loop?
choices: Setting B[k] to C[i] or D[j]
Copying all of C into a temporary array
questions.explain: Each iteration counts 4 operations: increment k, compare C[i] with D[j], write B[k], and increment i or j. MERGE makes no recursive calls.

questions.q: How does the work of merging two sorted arrays grow with their combined length n?
questions.explain: MERGE does 4n + 2 ≤ 6n operations. Merging two sorted arrays takes linear time.

questions.q: At level j of Merge Sort's recursion tree (the root is level 0), how many subproblems are there?
questions.explain: Each call makes 2 recursive calls, so the number of subproblems doubles at every level: 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^j.

questions.q: At level j of Merge Sort's recursion tree, how large is each subproblem?
questions.explain: The size halves at each level: n, n/2, n/4, ..., n/2^j.

questions.q: Using Lemma 1, what bound do you get on the total work at level j?
questions.explain: There are 2^j subproblems, and each does at most 6(n/2^j) work. The 2^j cancels, leaving at most 6n.

questions.q: Why is the work bound the same, 6n, at every level of Merge Sort's recursion tree?
choices: The number of subproblems doubles exactly as fast as each subproblem's size halves
Every level has exactly n subproblems
MERGE does a constant amount of work regardless of input size
Deeper levels skip the merge step
questions.explain: 2^j subproblems times 6n/2^j work each: the growth in count and the shrinking in size cancel.

questions.q: For n = 16, how many levels does Merge Sort's recursion tree have, counting level 0?
For n = 16, what is the Lemma 1 bound on the total work done at level 2 of the recursion tree?
questions.explain: Level 2 has 4 subproblems of size 4. Each does at most 6·4 = 24 work, so the total is at most 96 = 6·16.

questions.q: For n = 16, how many subproblems are at level 3 of the recursion tree?
questions.explain: 2^3 = 8 subproblems, each of size 16/8 = 2.

questions.q: Theorem 1 bounds the operations Merge Sort performs by 6n log₂ n + 6n. What is that bound for n = 8?
questions.explain: 6·8·3 + 6·8 = 144 + 48 = 192. Equivalently, 6n per level times (log₂ 8 + 1) = 4 levels: 48·4 = 192.

questions.q: One analysis says Merge Sort's recursion tree has log₂ n levels, and another says log₂ n + 1. Which is right?
choices: Both: log₂ n + 1 counts every level including level 0, while log₂ n counts the halvings; both are Θ(log n)
Only log₂ n, because level 0 does no work
Only log₂ n + 1, because log₂ n is an arithmetic mistake
Neither, because the tree has n levels
questions.explain: Halving n, n/2, ..., 1 takes log₂ n steps, giving log₂ n + 1 levels if you include the root. The exact proof of Theorem 1 uses log₂ n + 1.

questions.q: Which recurrence describes Merge Sort's running time?
questions.explain: There are two recursive calls on halves, plus linear work to merge.

questions.q: In T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), what does the 2T(n/2) term represent?
choices: Two recursive subproblems, each half the size
Two passes of MERGE over the whole array
Doubling the input size at each level
questions.explain: The coefficient 2 is the number of recursive calls (2 children per node in the tree). The n/2 is the halving, which gives log₂ n levels.

questions.q: In T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), what does the Θ(n) term represent?
choices: The work to merge the two sorted halves
The cost of the two recursive calls
The number of levels in the recursion tree
The cost of the base case
questions.explain: Θ(n) is the linear-time MERGE work done at each call.

questions.q: Drop constants and lower-order terms from the bound 6n log₂ n + 6n. What is Merge Sort's running time?
questions.explain: 6n is lower order than 6n log₂ n, and the constant 6 is dropped, leaving Θ(n log n).

questions.q: For n = 8, there are log₂ 8 levels of division, and about 8 elements are processed at each level. About how much total work is that?
questions.explain: 8 + 8 + 8 = 24, which matches n log₂ n = 8·3.

questions.q: Which principle does Merge Sort's analysis demonstrate?
choices: Doing a small amount of work across many levels can be much more efficient than doing a large amount of work within one level
Recursive algorithms are always faster than iterative ones
No sorting algorithm can run faster than Θ(n²)
The more levels a recursion tree has, the faster the algorithm
questions.explain: Merge Sort does only Θ(n) work per level across only Θ(log n) levels, for Θ(n log n) total.

questions.q: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n²), how many levels does the recursion tree have?
choices: log₂ n + 1, the same shape as Merge Sort's tree
2 log₂ n + 1, because the cost is squared
questions.explain: The tree still has 2 subproblems of half the size at each step, so its shape matches Merge Sort's. Only the cost per node changes.

questions.q: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n²), how much work is done at level j (ignoring constants)?
questions.explain: 2^j subproblems of size n/2^j, each costing (n/2^j)², gives 2^j · n²/4^j = n²/2^j. The work halves at each level.

questions.q: What is the overall running time for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n²)?
questions.explain: n²(1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ...) < 2n², and level 0 alone is n². The top level dominates, so the total is Θ(n²).

questions.q: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n²), multiplying level 0's work by the number of levels gives the tight answer Θ(n² log n).
questions.explain: That shortcut only works when every level does the same work, as in Merge Sort. Here the work halves at each level, so the levels sum to less than 2n² and the answer is Θ(n²).

questions.q: Suppose a subproblem of size m costs exactly m² in T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n². For n = 8, what is the total work summed over levels 0 through 3?
questions.explain: Level 0: 8² = 64. Level 1: 2·4² = 32. Level 2: 4·2² = 16. Level 3: 8·1² = 8. The total is 120, which is under 2n² = 128.
